title: Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow
hookLine: English Catholics executed for their faith under Elizabeth I

cards: A knock at the door of a house in York. Somewhere inside there's a hidden place where a priest can disappear, and a place to keep the things needed for Mass. The woman of the house runs a butcher's shop with her husband.
Her name is Margaret Clitherow. In the England of Elizabeth the First, sheltering a Catholic priest is a crime that can be punished by death.
Earlier, a scholar from Oxford named Edmund Campion rode from house to house in disguise, saying Mass in homes like hers.

teach.b: Edmund Campion was a brilliant Oxford man, admired at court. He became Catholic, joined the Jesuits abroad, and came back to England secretly, knowing what it might cost.
He preached in private houses and moved on before he could be caught. In a letter to the queen's council, he wrote that the cost had been counted and the work begun, and could not be stopped.
He was arrested, tortured, tried for treason, and executed. At his trial he argued that in condemning him, they condemned their own ancestors, whose faith he shared.
Catholic families built hiding places into their houses, so priests could vanish when searchers came.

Margaret Clitherow, the butcher's wife, hid priests in York. When she was arrested, she refused to enter a plea, so there would be no trial at which her children and household could be made to testify.
For refusing, the law of the time had her crushed to death. Then, the honest frame.
In that century, Christians of different churches put one another to death, in England and elsewhere. Protestants died under Catholic rulers too.
The Church honors its martyrs, and in our own time has also asked forgiveness for violence done in its name.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THEY THAT SUFFER PERSECUTION.
teach.b: The Gospel that Campion and Clitherow held to says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

how: Catholics honor Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow among the canonized martyrs of England and Wales, and some old English houses still show visitors their hidden priest holes.

practice: Bring to mind people somewhere in the world today who are in danger for what they believe, or for what they don't, any faith, any place, and simply hold them: the ones hiding, the ones in prison, the families waiting for news.
If you pray, pray for them, and for those who persecute them, as Jesus asked. If you don't, simply wish them safety and freedom.
